extracted.intended_audience: American colonists, colonial leaders, and the general public debating separation from Great Britain (readers of a political pamphlet)
extracted.subtask_description: A persuasive political pamphlet addressed to the inhabitants and representatives of the American colonies arguing for renunciation of dependence on Great Britain and proposing concrete structures and principles for a Continental government (assemblies, representation, charter, and defense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Renounce dependence on Great Britain / pursue independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any submission to, or dependence on, Great Britain, tends directly to involve this Continent in European wars and quarrels; it is the true interest of America to steer clear of European contentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments and evidence: commerce will secure peace and friendship of Europe; America's lack of gold and silver protects from invaders; British connection produces innumerable injuries and disadvantages; reconciliation is temporary and will likely result in ruin. Use moral, economic, and strategic reasoning to show independence is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partial connections; maintain neutrality in European affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: As Europe is our market for trade, we ought to form no partial connection with any part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial attachment to Britain makes America the 'make-weight' in British politics and will drag the Continent into European wars; neutrality and broad commerce are preferable for security and prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure ends against expense (proportionality of object to cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: The object contended for, ought always to bear some just proportion to the expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expend vast blood and treasure merely to achieve minor objectives (e.g., removing a contemptible ministry or temporarily stopping trade); weigh whether the desired political concession justifies the national cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual assemblies with a single president and domestic jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the assemblies be annual, with a president only. The representation more equal, their business wholly domestic, and subject to the authority of a Continental Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblies should focus on local/domestic matters, have regular (annual) sessions, and operate under an overarching Continental authority to preserve unity and prevent provincialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative apportionment: districting and minimum delegation sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Let each Colony be divided into six, eight, or ten convenient districts, each district to send a proper number of Delegates to Congress, so that each Colony send at least thirty. The whole number in Congress will be at least 390.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide colonies into convenient districts to equalize representation; ensure a substantial minimum delegation per colony so Congress represents the whole continent numerically and substantively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential selection by lotting colonies and rotating presidency
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Delegates are met, let a Colony be taken from the whole thirteen Colonies by lot, after which let the Congress choose (by ballot) a president from out of the Delegates of that Province. In the next Congress, omit that Colony in the lot, and proceed until all thirteen have had rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use random selection of a colony to limit concentration of power and ensure rotation and fairness in presidential origin; choose the president from that colony's delegates by ballot to combine chance with electoral choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supermajority threshold for passing laws: three-fifths
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that nothing may pass into a law but what is satisfactorily just, not less than three fifths of the Congress to be called a majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a higher-than-simple-majority threshold (3/5) to ensure greater consensus for legislation and to prevent ill-judged measures from becoming law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a Continental Conference with specified composition to draft a charter
rubrics_metrics.description: A Committee of twenty-six members of congress, viz. Two for each Colony. Two Members from each House of Assembly, or Provincial Convention: and five Representatives of the people at large, to be chosen in the capital city or town of each Province ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble an intermediate body combining experienced national representatives and popular delegates to draft foundational documents; specify exact representation types (Congress, assemblies, and people-at-large) to unite knowledge and legitimate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference duty: frame a Continental Charter (Magna Charta) with enumerated contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Let their business be to frame a Continental Charter, or Charter of the United Colonies; fixing the number and manner of choosing Members of Congress, Members of Assembly, with their date of sitting; and drawing the line of business and jurisdiction between them... Securing freedom and property to all men, and above all things, the free exercise of religion, according to the dictates of conscience; with such other matter as it is necessary for a charter to contain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The charter should (a) formalize representation and schedules, (b) delineate jurisdiction between continental and provincial bodies, and (c) guarantee individual rights (freedom, property, religious liberty). Emphasize continental strength over provincial interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic proclamation practice for the charter: law is king
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a day be solemnly set apart for proclaiming the Charter; let it be brought forth placed on the Divine Law, the Word of God; let a crown be placed thereon, by which the world may know, that so far as we approve of monarchy, that in America the law is king. ... the Crown at the conclusion of the ceremony be demolished, and scattered among the people whose right it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ceremonial acts to communicate constitutional principles: elevate law (and divine law) above rulers, symbolically reject monarchy by destroying the crown, and involve the people in the rite to legitimize the charter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: in free countries the law ought to be king
rubrics_metrics.description: For, as in absolute governments the King is law, so in free countries the law ought to be king; and there ought to be no other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground governance in the supremacy of law rather than a sovereign person; design institutions so law, not rulers, constrains and directs political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence as the means to domestic peace and to prevent civil wars
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but independance, i. e. a Continental form of government, can keep the peace of the Continent and preserve it inviolate from civil wars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that a stable continental government offering equality (no distinctions) prevents internal rivalries; claims republics (e.g., Holland, Switzerland) are peaceful, while monarchies provoke wars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval policy: build a fleet using domestic resources as commerce and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to view the building a fleet as an article of commerce, it being the natural manufactory of this country. 'Tis the best money we can lay out. A navy when finished is worth more than it cost. Let us build; if we want them not, we can sell; and by that means replace our paper currency with ready gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use America's native supplies (tar, timber, iron, cordage) to build a navy that doubles as industry and defense; treat shipbuilding as commerce that can be monetized if surplus. Includes cost accounting and comparisons to British navy expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manning the fleet: proportion of sailors not necessarily large
rubrics_metrics.description: In point of manning a fleet, people in general run into great errors; it is not necessary that one-fourth part should be sailors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions against assumptions about manpower composition of a fleet; implies flexible manning solutions (excerpt is truncated here but warns against fixed proportions).

rubrics_metrics.name: National debt policy: a national debt is not inherently a grievance
rubrics_metrics.description: No nation ought to be without a debt. A national debt is a national bond; and when it bears no interest, is in no case a grievance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframes national debt as a form of national credit that can finance a navy and provide value; compares favorably to Britain's large debt supporting a navy.
